title: Normal schemes with locally finitely many components are disjoint unions of normal integral components
statement: Let $X$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] such that every quasi-compact open [def-weil-pbc-quasi-compact-scheme] has finitely many irreducible components [def-weil-irreducible-components]. Suppose every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Then the irreducible components $Z_i\subseteq X$, indexed by a set $I$, are pairwise disjoint open and closed subsets covering $X$. With their induced open subscheme structures, the $Z_i$ are integral schemes [def-pc-integral-scheme] whose local rings are integrally closed domains. These open structures equal their reduced induced closed subscheme structures [def-pc-reduced-scheme, lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]. The canonical map $\coprod_{i\in I}Z_i\to X$ [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-coproduct-family] is an isomorphism. No local Noetherianity or quasi-compactness of $X$ is assumed; $I$ may be infinite, and is empty when $X$ is empty.

source.place: Tag 0357, label lemma-normal-locally-finite-nr-irreducibles, implication (1) to (2) and final paragraph of proof. The reduced induced structure agrees with the open structure because the latter is reduced and has the same closed support.

proof.text: Choose an affine open covering by lem-weil-pbc-affine-opens-basis. For any member $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$, lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs makes $U$ quasi-compact, so the hypothesis gives finitely many irreducible components of $U$. By lem-weil-pbc-spec-irreducible-components-minimal-primes they are the sets $V(\mathfrak p)$ for the minimal primes of $R$. This correspondence is injective: equality of the zero loci implies both prime inclusions by testing membership of $\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak q$ themselves. Thus $R$ has finitely many minimal primes. Domain stalks have no nonzero nilpotents, so $X$ is reduced; the open-section characterization in def-pc-reduced-scheme implies that $R$ is reduced. Finally every prime localization $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is the corresponding local ring of $X$, by lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization(c). Each is an integrally closed domain, so $R$ is a normal ring in the definition of def-weil-pbc-normal-ring.

proof.text: Apply implication (1) to (3) of lem-weil-pbc-reduced-normal-iff-integrally-closed-total-fractions to this $R$. Step 1 verifies all three hypotheses: reducedness, finitely many minimal primes, and normality. Obtain a ring isomorphism $R\simeq\prod_{a\in\operatorname{Fin}(n)}A_a$ with every $A_a$ a normal domain. The theorem allows $n=0$, which gives the zero ring and the empty affine open. No ring or scheme Noetherian hypothesis has entered.

proof.text:
Transport prime ideals through the ring isomorphism of Step 2; inverse image preserves inclusion and the sets defined by containment or noncontainment of an element. We can therefore calculate components in the finite product itself. Write $e_a$ for its coordinate idempotents and $K_a=\ker(R	o A_a)=(1-e_a)R$. Every prime $\mathfrak p$ contains exactly one of $e_a$ and $1-e_a$; since $\sum_a e_a=1$ and $e_ae_b=0$ for $a
e b$, exactly one $e_a$ is outside $\mathfrak p$. Thus every prime contains exactly one $K_a$. Each $K_a$ is prime because $A_a$ is a domain, and is minimal: if a prime $\mathfrak q\subseteq K_a$ contains $K_b$, then $b
e a$ is impossible since $e_a\in K_b$ but $e_a
otin K_a$; hence $\mathfrak q=K_a$. These are all minimal primes. Consequently the cited spectrum-component correspondence identifies the irreducible components of $U$ as $V(K_a)=D(e_a)$. Indeed $K_a=(1-e_a)R$ lies in a prime exactly when $e_a$ does not: the prime contains exactly one of the complementary idempotents. Hence $V(K_a)=D(e_a)$. These sets are pairwise disjoint, cover $U$, and are clopen, being both closed zero loci and basic opens. When $n=0$ there are no primes and no components.

proof.text: For any open $U\subseteq X$, intersection with $U$ carries global irreducible components meeting $U$ bijectively to the irreducible components of $U$. Indeed lem-weil-pbc-open-subspace-irreducible-closed-correspondence gives inverse order-preserving operations intersection and closure on irreducible closed subsets. If $T$ is a component meeting $U$ and $T\cap U\subseteq D$ with $D$ irreducible closed in $U$, then $T\subseteq\overline D$ and maximality gives $\overline D=T$, hence $D=T\cap U$. Conversely, for a component $D$ of $U$, its irreducible closure is contained in a component $T$ of $X$ by lem-sc-irreducible-components-cover. Then $D\subseteq T\cap U$ and maximality in $U$ gives equality, so taking closures gives $\overline D=T$. This also proves uniqueness, since the closure of $T\cap U$ is $T$.

source.place: Tag 0357, lemma-normal-locally-finite-nr-irreducibles, proof of (1) implies (2); general case, sentence concerning the intersections of a component with the affine covering; Topology Tag 0B7I (lemma-dimension-supremum-local-dimensions) and Tag 004W (lemma-irreducible)

proof.text: Let $T$ be a global irreducible component. On every affine member $U$ of the covering, $T\cap U$ is either empty or one of the clopen components calculated in Step 3. Thus $T$ is open, since its intersections with an open covering are open; it is closed by the definition of irreducible component. If global components $T,T^{\prime}$ meet at $x$, choose an affine $U$ containing $x$. Their traces are affine components meeting at $x$, hence are equal by Step 3; Step 4 then gives $T=T^{\prime}$. Every point belongs to a component by lem-sc-irreducible-components-cover. Hence the components are a pairwise disjoint clopen covering. They form a set because they are subsets of the set of points of $X$.

source.place: Tag 0357, lemma-normal-locally-finite-nr-irreducibles, proof of (1) implies (2); final paragraph, openness and disjoint covering

proof.text: Give a component $T$ its open subscheme structure $Z$. An open immersion identifies the structure sheaf with the restricted ambient sheaf (def-weil-open-immersion), so its stalk at each $x\in T$ is $\mathcal O_{X,x}$: the neighborhoods contained in $T$ are cofinal among the neighborhoods of $x$. Thus all stalks of $Z$ are integrally closed domains. In particular they are reduced, and def-pc-reduced-scheme makes $Z$ reduced. It is nonempty and irreducible by the component definition, so the reduced-and-irreducible characterization in def-pc-integral-scheme makes $Z$ integral. No assertion that an intersection of two affine opens is affine is needed.

source.place: Tag 0357, lemma-normal-locally-finite-nr-irreducibles, proof of (1) implies (2); final paragraph, integrality and normality of the open components; Tag 01ON (lemma-characterize-integral)

proof.text: The inclusion $j:Z\to X$ is also a closed immersion. Its underlying map is a homeomorphism onto the closed subset $T$. For every open $W\subseteq X$, the restriction $\mathcal O_X(W)\to\mathcal O_Z(W\cap T)$ is surjective: extend a section on $W\cap T$ by zero on $W\setminus T$ using the sheaf axiom on this disjoint open covering of $W$. Thus the structure-sheaf map is surjective, exactly the closed-immersion criterion of def-weil-closed-immersion. By Step 6 the source is reduced. Apply the uniqueness clause (3) of lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme to this reduced closed immersion with support $T$. It identifies the open structure with the reduced induced closed structure, as closed subschemes over $X$.

source.place: Tag 01J3, lemma-reduced-closed-subscheme, uniqueness; Tag 01J4, definition-reduced-induced-scheme; the clopen case of Properties Tag 0357

proof.text: Let $C=\coprod_{i\in I}Z_i$ with injections $k_i$, using lem-weil-pbc-scheme-coproduct-family, and let $p:C\to X$ be induced by the inclusions $j_i:Z_i\to X$. On the disjoint open cover $X=\bigcup_i Z_i$, the morphisms $k_i:Z_i\to C$ agree on overlaps because those overlaps are empty. The existence part of lem-weil-pbc-scheme-morphism-gluing gives $q:X\to C$ with $qj_i=k_i$. Then $pq$ restricts to $j_i$ on every $Z_i$, so the uniqueness part gives $pq=1_X$. Also $qpk_i=qj_i=k_i$ for all $i$, so the coproduct universal property gives $qp=1_C$. Hence $p$ is the asserted canonical isomorphism. For $X=\varnothing$ there is no nonempty irreducible subset, so $I=\varnothing$ and the same empty-cover and coproduct argument applies. Nothing uses finiteness of $I$.
